cards.meaning: have a short catch-up to check where things stand
cards.scenario: You want a five-minute check-in without calling it a meeting.
cards.example: Let's touch base on Thursday before the client call.

skill.work: Let's touch base after the client call to see where we stand.
skill.everyday: I'll touch base with Rahul on WhatsApp about Sunday's plan.
skill.analogy: Like a quick phone call home: two minutes to check everyone's fine, not a long chat.
skill.insteadOf: Can we have one small meeting to discuss the status?

cards.meaning: include someone in a conversation they should be part of
cards.scenario: A decision is being made without the person who owns the outcome.
cards.example: Let's loop Priya in before we finalise the dates.

skill.work: Please loop Arjun in — he owns the release date.
skill.everyday: Loop Riya in on the trip so she knows the plan.
skill.analogy: Like adding a cousin to the family group chat before the decision, not after.
skill.insteadOf: Please include Arjun in this discussion also.

cards.meaning: a rough estimate, not a committed number
cards.scenario: Someone wants a number now and you don't want it treated as final.
cards.example: Ballpark figure — about three weeks, but don't hold me to it.

skill.work: Give me a ballpark figure — how many days will testing take?
skill.everyday: Ballpark figure, how many people are coming to the Diwali party?
skill.analogy: Like guessing the auto fare before the meter starts: close enough to plan, not exact.

cards.meaning: a detailed examination of one thing
cards.scenario: A summary isn't enough and someone needs to go through it properly.
cards.example: Let's do a deep dive on churn next week.

skill.work: Next week, let's do a deep dive on why users drop off.
skill.everyday: Before buying the phone, my brother did a deep dive on every review.
skill.analogy: A summary is the match score; a deep dive is watching every ball of the innings.
skill.insteadOf: Let's discuss this topic in a very detailed manner.

cards.meaning: lost in detail, at the cost of the bigger picture
cards.scenario: A discussion has drifted into details nobody in the room needs.
cards.example: We're in the weeds — let's come back up a level.

skill.work: We're in the weeds on button colours — back to the launch plan.
skill.everyday: Planning the trip, we got in the weeds over seat numbers.
skill.analogy: Like arguing about the chutney while the guests are already at the door.
skill.insteadOf: We are going too much into the details.

cards.phrase: get our ducks in a row
cards.meaning: get everything organised before starting
cards.scenario: You want preparation finished before a launch or a big meeting.
cards.example: Let's get our ducks in a row before we present this.

skill.work: Let's get our ducks in a row before Friday's client demo.
skill.everyday: Get your ducks in a row — passport, tickets, hotel — before the trip.
skill.analogy: Like laying out every ingredient before you light the stove for biryani.
skill.insteadOf: Let's do all the preparation properly first.

cards.meaning: something you are aware of and watching
cards.scenario: Someone raises an issue you already know about but haven't acted on.
cards.example: It's on my radar — I just haven't got to it yet.

skill.work: The login bug is on my radar — I'll pick it up after lunch.
skill.everyday: Your cousin's birthday is on my radar; I've already ordered the cake.
skill.analogy: Like a train on the station board: you've seen it coming before it arrives.
skill.insteadOf: Yes, I know about it, I am aware.

cards.meaning: start again from the beginning after an approach failed
cards.scenario: The plan was rejected and there's no salvaging it.
cards.example: They said no to all three options, so it's back to the drawing board.

skill.work: The client rejected all three designs, so it's back to the drawing board.
skill.everyday: The cake sank in the middle — back to the drawing board.
skill.analogy: Like a dish that tastes wrong: you don't add more salt, you start cooking again.
skill.insteadOf: We have to start everything again from zero.

cards.meaning: skip proper steps to save time or money
cards.scenario: You're warning that speed is costing quality.
cards.example: We can hit the date, but only if we cut corners — I'd rather not.

skill.work: We can't cut corners on testing — this goes to every customer.
skill.everyday: The builder cut corners, so the bathroom leaked in the first monsoon.
skill.analogy: Like a cook skipping the slow fry of onions: faster, but everyone tastes the difference.
skill.insteadOf: We did it fast, but we skipped some steps.

cards.meaning: set a higher standard than before
cards.scenario: A piece of work is so good it changes what everyone expects.
cards.example: That presentation raised the bar for the whole team.

skill.work: Priya's report raised the bar for every review this quarter.
skill.everyday: My sister's Diwali rangoli raised the bar for the whole building.
skill.analogy: Like a high-jump bar moved up a notch: everyone after you must jump higher.

cards.meaning: start being productive immediately, with no ramp-up
cards.scenario: Describing someone new who needed no hand-holding.
cards.example: She hit the ground running in her first week.

skill.work: Fatima hit the ground running and shipped a fix in her first week.
skill.everyday: He moved to Pune and hit the ground running: found a flat in two days.
skill.analogy: Like a batsman who scores off the first ball instead of settling in for ten overs.
skill.insteadOf: She was productive from day one without any training.

cards.meaning: keep me updated as things develop
cards.scenario: You're handing something over but want to stay informed.
cards.example: You run with it — just keep me posted.

skill.work: You handle the vendor call — just keep me posted.
skill.everyday: Your train's late? Keep me posted so I know when to pick you up.
skill.analogy: Like live cricket score updates: you're not at the ground, but you hear every wicket.
skill.insteadOf: Please keep updating me about the same.

cards.meaning: a small change with visible benefit and little effort
cards.scenario: You want early progress people can see while the big work continues.
cards.example: Let's find a quick win for this week to keep everyone with us.

skill.work: Fixing the slow search page is a quick win for this sprint.
skill.everyday: Clearing the fridge was a quick win before the guests came.
skill.analogy: Like taking an easy single early in the innings: small, but it gets the board moving.
skill.insteadOf: This is a small task that will show results fast.

cards.meaning: many interconnected pieces, so it's easy for something to slip
cards.scenario: Explaining why something is riskier than it looks.
cards.example: There are a lot of moving parts here — I'd build in a buffer.

skill.work: The launch has a lot of moving parts, so let's add a buffer week.
skill.everyday: A wedding has a lot of moving parts — caterer, tent, band, guests.
skill.analogy: Like a train timetable: one late train and ten others are affected.
skill.insteadOf: This project is very complex with many things.

cards.meaning: set a topic aside deliberately, to return to later
cards.scenario: A valid point is derailing the agenda.
cards.example: Good point — let's park it and pick it up on Friday.

skill.work: Fair point — can we park it till the end of the meeting?
skill.everyday: Let's park the holiday talk till after Riya's exams.
skill.analogy: Like parking a car: it's not gone, just waiting while you do something else.
skill.insteadOf: Let's not discuss this now, we will discuss later.

cards.meaning: the value or skill someone contributes
cards.scenario: Explaining why someone should be part of a project.
cards.example: What he brings to the table is ten years of client relationships.

skill.work: Joseph brings real client experience to the table.
skill.everyday: In our cooking group, Fatima brings amazing biryani skills to the table.
skill.analogy: Like a potluck lunch: everyone brings one dish, and you ask what each one adds.
skill.insteadOf: He has a lot of good qualities for this project.

cards.phrase: the ball is in your court
cards.meaning: it's now your turn to act
cards.scenario: You've done your part and the next move belongs to someone else.
cards.example: I've sent the revised terms, so the ball is in their court.

skill.work: I've sent the revised plan, so the ball is in their court now.
skill.everyday: I've apologised to Rahul; the ball's in his court now.
skill.analogy: Like badminton: you've hit the shuttle over the net, and now it's their move.
skill.insteadOf: I did my part, now they have to do something.

cards.meaning: deprioritised, but not cancelled
cards.scenario: Something important has pushed a smaller project down the list.
cards.example: The rebrand is on the back burner until Q4.

skill.work: The new dashboard is on the back burner until the launch is done.
skill.everyday: Learning guitar is on the back burner while the baby is small.
skill.analogy: Like a pot of dal on the back burner: still cooking, just not getting attention.
skill.insteadOf: This work is pending for now, we will see later.

cards.meaning: fully informed and able to contribute
cards.scenario: Someone is joining a project that's already running.
cards.example: Give me a day to get up to speed and I'll take it from there.

skill.work: Can you get Arjun up to speed before he joins the client call?
skill.everyday: I missed the family group chat — can someone get me up to speed?
skill.analogy: Like joining a moving train: you run alongside till you match its speed, then hop on.
skill.insteadOf: Please tell him all the old details of the project.

cards.meaning: applying to everyone or everything, with no exceptions
cards.scenario: A change affects every team, not just one.
cards.example: Costs are up across the board, not just in our function.

skill.work: Response times improved across the board, not just on mobile.
skill.everyday: Prices at the vegetable market went up across the board this week.
skill.analogy: Like a power cut in the whole colony, not just your flat.
skill.insteadOf: This change is for all the teams, everyone.

cards.meaning: strictly following the official rules
cards.scenario: A situation is sensitive enough that no shortcuts are acceptable.
cards.example: This one we do by the book — every approval documented.

skill.work: It's an audit, so we do it by the book: every approval in writing.
skill.everyday: The new driving instructor does everything by the book.
skill.analogy: Like a strict umpire: no shortcuts, every rule applied, even when nobody's watching.
skill.insteadOf: We will follow all the rules and procedures properly.

cards.meaning: a rare situation at the limits of normal use
cards.scenario: Someone objects with an unlikely scenario.
cards.example: That's an edge case — let's handle the common path first.

skill.work: Leap-year birthdays are an edge case — let's fix the common path first.
skill.everyday: Twelve surprise guests is an edge case, but let's keep extra rice anyway.
skill.analogy: Like planning a picnic for the rare day it hails in May: possible, not the first worry.
skill.insteadOf: This is a very rare scenario, it won't come usually.

cards.meaning: formally approve something to proceed
cards.scenario: A decision-maker has finally approved a plan.
cards.example: Finance gave it the green light this morning.

skill.work: Our manager gave the green light, so we start the pilot on Monday.
skill.everyday: Mum gave the green light for the Goa trip!
skill.analogy: Like a traffic signal turning green: everyone was waiting, now you can go.
skill.insteadOf: Finance has given the approval for going ahead.

cards.meaning: do more than was required
cards.scenario: Recognising someone who did more than their job asked.
cards.example: She went the extra mile on that handover.

skill.work: Riya went the extra mile and wrote a guide for the new joiners.
skill.everyday: The shopkeeper went the extra mile and carried the gas cylinder upstairs himself.
skill.analogy: Like an auto driver who drops you at your gate, not at the main road.
skill.insteadOf: She did more work than what was given to her.

cards.meaning: kept informed as part of a group
cards.scenario: You want to stay informed without owning the work.
cards.example: I don't need to be in every meeting, just keep me in the loop.

skill.work: I don't need every meeting — just keep me in the loop by email.
skill.everyday: Keep me in the loop about the reunion, even if I can't come.
skill.analogy: Like being cc'd on an email: you're not doing the work, but you see every update.
skill.insteadOf: Please inform me about everything that is happening.

cards.meaning: unlikely to succeed, but worth trying
cards.scenario: Proposing something with low odds and low cost.
cards.example: It's a long shot, but I'll ask them anyway.

skill.work: It's a long shot, but let's ask if the client can move the date.
skill.everyday: It's a long shot, but try for Tatkal tickets tomorrow morning.
skill.analogy: Like hoping for a six off the last ball: unlikely, but worth swinging for.
skill.insteadOf: The chances are low, but we can still try.

cards.meaning: an obvious decision requiring no thought
cards.scenario: The benefit is so clear that debating it wastes time.
cards.example: At that price it's a no-brainer.

skill.work: Reusing the old login screen is a no-brainer — it already works.
skill.everyday: Metro instead of an auto in Bengaluru traffic? A no-brainer.
skill.analogy: Like choosing hot chai on a rainy day: there's nothing to think about.
skill.insteadOf: This is a very obvious decision, no need to think.

cards.phrase: off the top of my head
cards.meaning: from memory, without checking
cards.scenario: Giving a number you don't want treated as verified.
cards.example: Off the top of my head, around forty accounts.

skill.work: Off the top of my head, about forty users reported it — I'll check.
skill.everyday: Off the top of my head, the shop closes at nine.
skill.analogy: Like giving directions from memory instead of opening Maps: probably right, not checked.
skill.insteadOf: I don't know exactly, but I think it's around forty.

cards.meaning: undecided between two options
cards.scenario: You genuinely haven't chosen and want more input.
cards.example: I'm on the fence — talk me through the second option again.

skill.work: I'm on the fence about the two vendors — can we compare them again?
skill.everyday: I'm on the fence about a new phone; my old one still works.
skill.analogy: Like standing at a chai stall, unable to pick between masala and ginger.
skill.insteadOf: I am confused which option to choose.

cards.meaning: decide as you go rather than planning in advance
cards.scenario: There's too much uncertainty to commit to a plan now.
cards.example: Let's play it by ear and see how the first session goes.

skill.work: We don't know the client's mood, so let's play the meeting by ear.
skill.everyday: Dinner after the movie? Let's play it by ear.
skill.analogy: Like a musician without sheet music: you listen and adjust as you go.
skill.insteadOf: We will decide according to the situation at that time.

cards.meaning: stop something before it finishes
cards.scenario: A project isn't working and continuing would waste more.
cards.example: We pulled the plug after the second pilot.

skill.work: After two failed pilots, we pulled the plug on the chatbot.
skill.everyday: It rained all morning, so we pulled the plug on the picnic.
skill.analogy: Like switching off a running mixer: the job stops right there, finished or not.
skill.insteadOf: We stopped the project before it was finished.

cards.meaning: excessive official procedure that slows things down
cards.scenario: Explaining why something simple took a long time.
cards.example: The work took two days; the red tape took three weeks.

skill.work: The fix took a day; the red tape for approval took two weeks.
skill.everyday: Getting a new gas connection meant a month of red tape.
skill.analogy: Like a train ticket needing five stamps from five counters before you can board.
skill.insteadOf: There are too many formalities and procedures.

cards.meaning: waste effort rebuilding something that already exists
cards.scenario: Someone is about to build what another team already has.
cards.example: Marketing has a template — no need to reinvent the wheel.

skill.work: Design already has a template — no need to reinvent the wheel.
skill.everyday: Use Grandma's pickle recipe — don't reinvent the wheel.
skill.analogy: Like grinding your own flour when the shop down the road sells it fresh.
skill.insteadOf: Why make it again from scratch when it already exists?

cards.meaning: basically good, but unpolished
cards.scenario: Giving honest but fair feedback on early work.
cards.example: It's rough around the edges, but the thinking is right.

skill.work: The draft is rough around the edges, but the idea is strong.
skill.everyday: The new café is rough around the edges, but the coffee is great.
skill.analogy: Like a fresh clay pot before smoothing: the shape is right, the finish isn't.

cards.meaning: do the calculations before deciding
cards.scenario: An idea sounds good and nobody has checked whether it adds up.
cards.example: Let me run the numbers before we commit to that.

skill.work: Let me run the numbers before we promise the client a date.
skill.everyday: We ran the numbers, and the train works out cheaper than flying.
skill.analogy: Like checking the bill before you pay: a deal can look good until you add it up.
skill.insteadOf: Let me calculate everything and then tell you.

cards.meaning: agree fully with someone
cards.scenario: Describing a disagreement without making it personal.
cards.example: We don't see eye to eye on pricing, but that's fine.

skill.work: Arjun and I don't see eye to eye on the timeline, and that's fine.
skill.everyday: My dad and I don't see eye to eye on cricket captains.
skill.analogy: Like two umpires agreeing on every decision without checking the replay.
skill.insteadOf: We have a difference of opinion on this.

cards.meaning: give formal approval
cards.scenario: Nothing can proceed until a specific person approves.
cards.example: I need legal to sign off on the wording first.

skill.work: Can you sign off on the copy by noon so we can publish?
skill.everyday: Mum has to sign off on the menu before we order.
skill.analogy: Like a teacher's signature in the homework diary: nothing moves until it's there.
skill.insteadOf: Please give your approval for this content.

cards.meaning: accept full responsibility for something
cards.scenario: A task keeps slipping because nobody is clearly accountable.
cards.example: I'll take ownership of the migration end to end.

skill.work: I'll take ownership of the release notes from now on.
skill.everyday: My brother took ownership of the house repairs while Dad was away.
skill.analogy: Like the captain who says 'my call' and lives with the result.
skill.insteadOf: I will take care of this, don't worry.

cards.meaning: blame someone publicly to protect yourself
cards.scenario: Describing someone shifting blame in a meeting.
cards.example: He threw the whole team under the bus in that review.

skill.work: When the launch slipped, he threw the designers under the bus.
skill.everyday: When the vase broke, my brother threw me under the bus.
skill.analogy: Like a batsman who runs his partner out, then blames him for the call.
skill.insteadOf: He blamed others in front of everyone to save himself.

cards.meaning: something difficult that stays difficult throughout
cards.scenario: Setting expectations that progress will be slow and hard.
cards.example: Changing that habit across four teams is an uphill battle.

skill.work: Getting every team to write tests is an uphill battle.
skill.everyday: Getting Dad to use UPI was an uphill battle.
skill.analogy: Like cycling up a ghat road: every metre takes effort, and no downhill in sight.
skill.insteadOf: This is very difficult work, it will take time.

cards.meaning: information spread by people telling each other
cards.scenario: Explaining how something grew without advertising.
cards.example: Almost all of it came through word of mouth.

skill.work: Most of our first customers came through word of mouth.
skill.everyday: That dosa place has no sign; it runs on word of mouth.
skill.analogy: Like news in a housing society: no notice board needed, everyone just tells everyone.
skill.insteadOf: People told other people, and that is how it spread.

cards.meaning: please be patient for a moment
cards.scenario: You need a few seconds while something loads or you find a file.
cards.example: Bear with me — the file is opening.

skill.work: Bear with me — my screen share is loading.
skill.everyday: Bear with me, I'm finding the address on my phone.
skill.analogy: Like asking the auto driver to wait one minute while you grab your bag.
skill.insteadOf: Just one minute, please wait.

cards.meaning: reach a point where you can't make further progress
cards.scenario: You've exhausted your options and need help.
cards.example: I've hit a wall on this — can I borrow you for ten minutes?

skill.work: I've hit a wall with this bug — can you look at it with me?
skill.everyday: I hit a wall on the crossword and gave up.
skill.analogy: Like a car on a dead-end lane: the engine works, but there's nowhere left to go.
skill.insteadOf: I am stuck and I don't know what to do now.

cards.meaning: genuine agreement and support from the people involved
cards.scenario: A plan will fail unless the people affected actually want it.
cards.example: The plan is fine; we don't have buy-in from operations yet.

skill.work: We need buy-in from the support team before changing their tools.
skill.everyday: Getting the kids' buy-in made the new screen-time rule actually work.
skill.analogy: Like a family trip everyone voted on: nobody sulks in the car.
skill.insteadOf: The other team is not agreeing with our plan fully.

cards.meaning: finish an open item and tell everyone it's done
cards.scenario: Something was raised, resolved, and never reported back.
cards.example: I'll close the loop with the client this afternoon.

skill.work: I'll close the loop with the client once the fix is live.
skill.everyday: Close the loop with the plumber so he knows we don't need him.
skill.analogy: Like texting 'reached safely' after a trip, so nobody's left wondering.
skill.insteadOf: I will inform the client that the issue is solved.

cards.meaning: learn how things actually work in a new place
cards.scenario: Someone new is slow because nobody showed them the basics.
cards.example: Give her two weeks to learn the ropes before judging output.

skill.work: Give Arjun two weeks to learn the ropes before judging his work.
skill.everyday: My cousin is learning the ropes at his uncle's sweet shop.
skill.analogy: Like a new player in the team: first you learn where everyone fields.
skill.insteadOf: He is new, he is still understanding how things work here.

cards.meaning: start something that has been discussed too long
cards.scenario: A plan is fully discussed and nobody has taken the first step.
cards.example: Let's get the ball rolling with ten customer calls this week.

skill.work: Let's get the ball rolling with five customer calls this week.
skill.everyday: I'll get the ball rolling on the reunion by making the group.
skill.analogy: Like the first push on a stuck car: once it moves, it keeps moving.
skill.insteadOf: Let's start the work now, we discussed enough.

cards.meaning: do the extra work left by someone missing
cards.scenario: A teammate is on leave and their share still has to ship.
cards.example: Rahul is picking up the slack while Priya is on leave.

skill.work: Fatima is on leave, so Joseph is picking up the slack this week.
skill.everyday: When Mum's travelling, my sister picks up the slack at home.
skill.analogy: Like a fielder covering a teammate's area while he's off the field.
skill.insteadOf: He is doing her work also while she is on leave.

cards.meaning: skip the background and say the point
cards.scenario: An update is rambling and the room is losing patience.
cards.example: Let me cut to the chase — we need two more weeks.

skill.work: To cut to the chase, the release moves to Thursday.
skill.everyday: Cut to the chase — are you coming to the wedding or not?
skill.analogy: Like skipping the songs to reach the climax of the film.
skill.insteadOf: So basically, first let me tell you the full background...

cards.meaning: stop the small talk and start the real work
cards.scenario: Ten minutes of pleasantries and the agenda hasn't started.
cards.example: Good to see everyone — let's get down to business.

skill.work: Coffee's here, so let's get down to business on the roadmap.
skill.everyday: Enough chatting — let's get down to business and pack.
skill.analogy: Like the umpire calling 'play' after the toss and the photos.
skill.insteadOf: Okay, now we will start the actual discussion.

cards.meaning: the overall situation, not the details
cards.scenario: The team is fighting over pixels while the launch date burns.
cards.example: Forget the font for now — look at the big picture.

skill.work: Forget the font for now; the big picture is a Friday launch.
skill.everyday: Don't fight over seats — the big picture is a family holiday.
skill.analogy: Like the wide shot of the whole cricket ground instead of a close-up of one fielder.
skill.insteadOf: Let's think about the overall thing, not small things.

cards.meaning: the final result that actually matters
cards.scenario: A long debate needs one line that settles it.
cards.example: The bottom line is we ship Friday, with or without the animation.

skill.work: The bottom line is the client needs it by March.
skill.everyday: The bottom line is we leave by six or we miss the train.
skill.analogy: Like the final score: the commentary is interesting, but the score decides.
skill.insteadOf: The final conclusion of all this is...

cards.meaning: be the one who makes the final decisions
cards.scenario: Nobody knows who can actually approve the spend.
cards.example: On this project, the client calls the shots on scope.

skill.work: Our manager calls the shots on which features ship first.
skill.everyday: At home, Grandma calls the shots on the Diwali menu.
skill.analogy: Like the captain setting the field: others suggest, he decides.
skill.insteadOf: She is the one who takes all the final decisions.

cards.meaning: step forward and run with something
cards.scenario: A task has volunteers but no driver.
cards.example: I'll take the lead on the migration and report Fridays.

skill.work: I'll take the lead on the migration and update you every Friday.
skill.everyday: My sister took the lead on planning Dad's sixtieth birthday.
skill.analogy: Like the first car in a convoy: the others follow the route it picks.
skill.insteadOf: I will drive this task from my side.

cards.meaning: rise to the occasion when extra is needed
cards.scenario: Crunch week needs everyone doing a little more.
cards.example: The whole team stepped up during the outage.

skill.work: With two people on leave, the whole team stepped up.
skill.everyday: When the cook was off, my brother stepped up and made dinner.
skill.analogy: Like a tailender who scores runs when the top order collapses.
skill.insteadOf: Everyone did extra work at that time.

cards.meaning: directly doing the work, not just directing it
cards.scenario: A manager is seen as distant from the real work.
cards.example: She's very hands-on — she reviews every release herself.

skill.work: Riya is very hands-on — she tests every release herself.
skill.everyday: My dad is hands-on with the garden; he waters it every morning.
skill.analogy: Like a head chef who still tastes every dish, not just writes the menu.
skill.insteadOf: She does the work herself, not only giving instructions.

cards.meaning: the final stretch when everything must come together
cards.scenario: Three days to launch and the team needs focus, not new ideas.
cards.example: It's crunch time — no new features till we ship.

skill.work: It's crunch time — no new features until we ship.
skill.everyday: Exams start Monday, so it's crunch time for my sister.
skill.analogy: Like the last five overs of a run chase: every ball counts.
skill.insteadOf: Now the deadline is very near, we have less time.

cards.meaning: decided or finished at the last possible moment
cards.scenario: A negotiation runs into the final hour.
cards.example: The approval went down to the wire on Friday evening.

skill.work: The client deal went down to the wire on Friday evening.
skill.everyday: The cricket final went down to the wire — won on the last ball.
skill.analogy: Like a race decided right at the finishing line, not a metre earlier.
skill.insteadOf: It was finished at the very last moment.

cards.meaning: at the last possible moment before it's too late
cards.scenario: A rescue arrives just before the deadline.
cards.example: Legal cleared it at the eleventh hour.

skill.work: Legal approved the contract at the eleventh hour.
skill.everyday: He found the ring at the eleventh hour, just before the engagement.
skill.analogy: Like jumping onto the train just as it pulls out of the platform.

cards.meaning: the agreed plan for winning something specific
cards.scenario: The team needs one shared plan before a big pitch.
cards.example: What's our game plan for the client demo tomorrow?

skill.work: What's our game plan for tomorrow's client demo?
skill.everyday: What's the game plan for Sunday — market first or lunch first?
skill.analogy: Like a team talk before the match: everyone knows their role.
skill.insteadOf: What is our strategy and plan of action for the demo?

cards.meaning: find ideas beyond the usual approaches
cards.scenario: Every obvious option has failed and the team is stuck.
cards.example: We need to think outside the box on distribution.

skill.work: We need to think outside the box to reach small-town users.
skill.everyday: No oven? Think outside the box — bake the cake in a pressure cooker.
skill.analogy: Like the kirana shop that took orders on WhatsApp before any app did.
skill.insteadOf: We need to think of some new and different ideas.

cards.meaning: a deal where both sides genuinely gain
cards.scenario: A negotiation is stuck because one side must lose.
cards.example: Let's find a win-win — faster payment for a small discount.

skill.work: If we share the test server, both teams save time — a win-win.
skill.everyday: You cook, I wash up — win-win.
skill.analogy: Like swapping tiffins at lunch: both of you get something you like.
skill.insteadOf: This deal is good for both of us.

cards.meaning: warn that something looks wrong or risky
cards.scenario: A vendor promise sounds too good and nobody has checked it.
cards.example: The missing paperwork raised a red flag for me.

skill.work: The vendor's missing references raised a red flag for me.
skill.everyday: A landlord who wants cash only? That raises a red flag.
skill.analogy: Like a red flag on the beach: it doesn't stop you, it warns you.
skill.insteadOf: I felt something is not right with this vendor.

cards.meaning: deliberately or carelessly not told what is happening
cards.scenario: A decision affecting your work was made without you.
cards.example: Don't keep support in the dark about the release date.

skill.work: The design team was kept in the dark about the new deadline.
skill.everyday: Everyone knew about the surprise party; I was kept in the dark.
skill.analogy: Like the one relative nobody told that the wedding date had changed.
skill.insteadOf: Nobody informed us about this decision.
